name: Celecoxib
summary: The COX-2-selective inhibitor that survived the 2004 safety re-evaluation — meaningfully lower GI risk than nonselective NSAIDs, without antiplatelet effect.
good: High GI-bleeding-risk patients (prior ulcer, elderly, concurrent anticoagulation) who need an NSAID and have low-to-moderate cardiovascular risk.
bad: Established cardiovascular disease, or when combined with low-dose aspirin — you gain the CV risk of COX-2 inhibition while gaining back the GI risk aspirin already carries.
clinicalPearls: Adding celecoxib on top of aspirin removes celecoxib’s main advantage: you now have aspirin’s GI risk plus celecoxib’s CV consideration, without either drug’s main benefit being clean.
mechanism: Selective inhibition of the inducible COX-2 isoform, largely sparing COX-1-mediated gastric mucosal protection and platelet thromboxane production.
originalFields: Selective inhibition of the inducible COX-2 isoform, largely sparing COX-1-mediated gastric mucosal protection and platelet thromboxane production.
Roughly 10–20x selective for COX-2 over COX-1 — meaningful, though less extreme than etoricoxib.
Substantially lower than nonselective NSAIDs, particularly for upper GI ulceration/bleeding.
Present, dose-dependent; framed by regulators as a class effect shared with (though sometimes less pronounced than) other COX-2-selective agents.
Same COX-2-mediated renal mechanism as nonselective NSAIDs — selectivity does not spare the kidney.

Does not inhibit platelet thromboxane A₂ — cannot substitute for aspirin’s cardioprotective effect, and does not counterbalance its own prothrombotic tendency the way aspirin’s antiplatelet action does.
